127.title: Your simran
127.hook: settle on a time and a length that fits your life
127.howItsDone: Sikhs keep simran in many ways: alone before dawn, in short moments through the day, or together in the gurdwara where the sangat repeats Waheguru in rhythm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simran while working, Namdev at his dyes. Your line was hands at work, heart at home. Which task did you let the quiet word run under? Day one hundred twenty-seven.
screen: `SIMRAN WHILE WORKING — HANDS AT WORK, HEART AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Every January, someone at the gym promises themselves an hour a day, every day, forever. By February, the plan is gone. Not because they're lazy. Because the plan never fit their actual life. The same thing happens with prayer and meditation. It's easy to picture the ideal version, the saint up at three, sitting still for hours, and then to count anything less as failure. So today is the last day of this stretch on simran, and it's not about a new technique. It's about making a plan that fits you.
screen: `AN HOUR A DAY, FOREVER.` → `GONE BY FEBRUARY.` → `A PLAN THAT FITS YOUR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Look back at what this week gave you. Waheguru on the breath, Wahe in, Guru out. Satnam: true name. Coming back when the mind runs off. The early hour, amrit vela. The mala, bead by bead. And the Name running under your work. None of these are rules you must follow. They're tools. Sikhs use them in many combinations. Some do simran for an hour before dawn. Some do five minutes on the bus. Some join the sangat for simran together at the gurdwara, the whole room repeating Waheguru in rhythm. The Sikh code of conduct asks Sikhs to rise early and to meditate on the Name, and many take that as a daily anchor, but the Gurus never set a minimum number of minutes. What the Guru Granth Sahib does keep returning to is remembering, and remembering is something done again and again, not once in a heroic burst. So here are three questions for your simran. When? Pick a time that already exists in your day: waking up, a coffee, a commute, before sleep. Where? A real place: the edge of the bed, a chair, the car before you go in. How long? Start smaller than you think. Five minutes, done every day, beats an hour done once. And if a day gets missed, simran has its own answer for that too. You just come back.
screen: `A WEEK OF TOOLS, NOT RULES.` · `NO MINIMUM MINUTES.` · `STEADINESS OVER HEROICS.` · `WHEN, WHERE, HOW LONG.` · then, large: `YOUR FIVE MINUTES.`

segments.voice: Choose your five minutes now. Close your eyes and walk through tomorrow in your mind, from waking up. Where's a gap? Maybe it's before you check your phone, or right after you drop the kids, or when you park the car. Pick one. Picture yourself there, doing five minutes of whichever simran you liked best this week. If you're here to learn, choose five minutes of quiet breathing instead. Stay in that picture. The bell holds the time.
Your simran. Remembering the Name, at a time, a place and a length that fit your real life, done steadily.
Your line: your five minutes. Tell one person, or write on a sticky note, when and where your five minutes will be. Then keep it tomorrow. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: The daily banis
128.hook: Nitnem means daily practice: set prayers at dawn, at dusk and at night
128.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Nitnem daily: Japji, Jaap and the Savaiyas (and often Chaupai and Anand) in the morning, Rehras Sahib at sunset and Kirtan Sohila before sleep, from memory, from a gutka or along with a recording.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your simran, and a plan that fits your life. Your line was your five minutes. Did you keep them this morning? If not, there's always coming back. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

A daily routine can run almost unnoticed. Coffee before anything. The same podcast on the drive. Checking the locks at night. Those small repeated things hold a day together, like the hinges on a door. Sikhs have a routine like this too, but it's made of words. At dawn, at dusk and at night, many Sikhs recite set hymns from the Gurus. Not new words each day. The same words, day after day, for years, until they're part of the person. Today we start a new stretch of the path: that daily routine of prayer.
screen: `COFFEE, PODCAST, LOCKS.` → `A ROUTINE MADE OF WORDS.` → `DAWN, DUSK AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The routine is called Nitnem. Nit means daily, always. Nem means a rule, a discipline, a vow you keep. So Nitnem is the daily discipline, and in practice it means a set of banis, hymns from the Gurus, said at fixed times. Bani simply means the word, the Guru's utterance. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, lays out three times. In the morning: Japji Sahib, by Guru Nanak, then Jaap Sahib and the ten Savaiyas, by Guru Gobind Singh. Many Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five banis in the morning, adding Chaupai Sahib and Anand Sahib. In the evening, at sunset: Rehras Sahib. And at night, before sleep: Kirtan Sohila, which you met on day one hundred thirteen. Morning, evening, night. Three doors in the day, each opened with the Guru's words. Some Sikh traditions and jathas include a few more banis or slightly longer versions, and we'll come to that. Why the same words every day? A path across a field works like this. The first time you walk it, it's just grass. Walk it every day and it becomes a path, and your feet find it in the dark. Daily banis can work like that on the mind. Over years, the lines surface on their own: in traffic, at a hospital bed, at a wedding. And Nitnem isn't only for the devout few. Children learn it at home, grandparents keep it, and many Sikhs listen along to a recording on the way to work. Over the coming days we'll meet each bani, plainly, one at a time.
screen: `NIT — DAILY. NEM — A DISCIPLINE.` · `MORNING: JAPJI, JAAP, SAVAIYAS.` · `EVENING REHRAS, NIGHT SOHILA.` · `A PATH WORN INTO THE FIELD.` · then, large: `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Learn the three times, in your own day. Close your eyes. Picture your morning: where are you right after you wake? That's the first door. Now picture your evening, as the light goes and work ends. The second door. Now picture the moment before sleep, lights off. The third door. Walk through them slowly, one at a time: morning, evening, night. You don't have to fill them with anything yet. Just notice that each one is there. The bell holds the time.
Nitnem. The daily discipline: set banis of the Gurus said at dawn, at dusk and at night.
Your line: morning, evening, night. Today, at each of those three doors, pause for one breath and notice that you've crossed it. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

129.title: Japji at dawn
129.hook: Guru Nanak's Japji is the first morning bani
129.howItsDone: Japji Sahib is the first bani of the Sikh morning; many Sikhs recite it from memory or from a gutka in the amrit vela, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nitnem, the daily banis. Your line was morning, evening, night. Did you notice crossing those three doors? Today we open the first one. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

Before sunrise in Sikh homes around the world, from Amritsar to Toronto to Nairobi, the same words are being said. A grandfather in a kitchen, murmuring from memory. A student with a small prayer book on her knee. A taxi driver with a recording playing low. For those who say it, it's the first thing the day hears. It's the same hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib itself. Page one. Today, Japji.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, EVERYWHERE.` → `THE FIRST THING THE DAY HEARS.` → `PAGE ONE OF THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Japji Sahib is by Guru Nanak. Jap means to recite, to repeat, to meditate on; ji and sahib are words of respect. So it's the honored recitation. It begins with the Mul Mantar, the root verse you know: Ik Onkar, Satnam, one God, whose name is truth. Then a short salok saying God was true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and will be true. Then come thirty-eight pauris, stanzas, and a closing salok. The first pauri is a surprise. Before telling you how to find God, Guru Nanak tells you what doesn't work. In paraphrase: thinking won't do it, even a hundred thousand times. Silence won't do it, even if you sit silent forever. Piling up the world's goods won't satisfy hunger. Thousands upon thousands of clever tricks, and not one goes with you. So how, then? His answer closes that stanza: by walking in the hukam, the Divine Order, the Will, which is written with us. From there, Japji travels through the whole of life: listening, trusting, the vastness of creation, and at the end five realms of the spirit, rising to the realm of truth. The last salok, in paraphrase, calls air the guru, water the father, and the great earth the mother, and day and night the two nurses in whose laps the whole world plays. One unusual detail: nearly every hymn in the Granth is set to a raag, a musical mode, for singing. Japji isn't. It's meant to be recited, spoken, the plain words at the start of the day. That's why Sikhs begin with Japji.
screen: `JAP — TO RECITE, TO MEDITATE.` · `THINKING WON'T DO IT.` · `WALK IN THE HUKAM.` · `AIR THE GURU, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH JAPJI.`

segments.voice: Listen to Japji's opening. If you can, find a recording of Japji Sahib now, and play the first minute or two: the Mul Mantar and the start of the first pauri. You don't need to understand the Punjabi. Just let the sound of it be the first thing in this moment, the way it is for many Sikhs at dawn. If you can't play it now, sit quietly and hear in your mind the two words you already know: Ik Onkar. The bell holds the time.
Japji at dawn. Guru Nanak's recitation, page one of the Guru Granth Sahib, the first bani of the Sikh morning.
Your line: begin with japji. Tomorrow morning, before the phone, before the news, listen to Japji's first minute. Let it be the first voice your day hears. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

130.title: Jaap Sahib
130.hook: Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise of the Timeless, in quick changing meters
130.howItsDone: Jaap Sahib, by Guru Gobind Singh, is the second bani of the Sikh morning Nitnem and is also recited during the Amrit ceremony; many Sikhs know its quick rhythms by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji at dawn, page one of the Granth. Your line was begin with japji. Did Japji get the first minute of your morning? Today, the bani that comes right after it. Day one hundred thirty.

You know how some music makes it impossible to sit still? A drumline at a parade. A song where the beat suddenly doubles and the whole crowd jumps. Japji is calm, like a teacher talking. The next bani in the Sikh morning is something else. It gallops. The lines are short, the rhythm keeps changing, and when a whole room recites it together it can feel like running downhill. It was written by the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh. Today, Jaap Sahib.
screen: `A DRUMLINE, A DOUBLED BEAT.` → `JAPJI IS CALM.` → `THE NEXT ONE GALLOPS.`

segments.voice: Jaap Sahib is a long hymn of praise, about two hundred short verses, by Guru Gobind Singh. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. It's in a separate collection called the Dasam Granth, the book of the tenth Guru, and it's said every morning in Nitnem and at the Amrit ceremony, when Sikhs are initiated into the Khalsa. It praises Akal, the Timeless One. And here's the unusual thing about how it praises. Much of it describes God by what God is not. The opening, in paraphrase: the One who has no mark or sign, no color, no caste, no lineage; whose form and shape and garb no one can describe. Then it rolls into salutations, line after line, each beginning with a word of bowing: salutation to the Timeless, salutation to the Merciful, salutation to the One without form, to the One without a name. Hundreds of names, most of them saying: beyond this, beyond that. It's as if the words keep reaching and keep admitting they can't reach. And the rhythm. Guru Gobind Singh was a poet as well as a leader, and he wrote Jaap in many different meters, chhands, switching from one to another as the hymn goes on. Some sections are slow and stately. Some are so quick the syllables tumble. The language mixes Braj, Sanskrit, Punjabi and even Persian and Arabic words, as if praise needed every language he knew. You don't have to follow the meaning to feel what it's doing. It's praise with a heartbeat, and the heartbeat keeps changing.
screen: `DASAM GRANTH, THE TENTH GURU.` · `NO MARK, NO SIGN, NO CASTE.` · `SALUTATION, SALUTATION.` · `MANY METERS, MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `THE RHYTHM OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Listen for two minutes. If you can, play a recording of Jaap Sahib now. Don't try to understand every word. Listen for the rhythm: when does it speed up? When does it slow down? Tap the beat lightly on your knee if that helps. If you can't play anything, sit and breathe, and notice your own rhythm, your heartbeat, your breath, the one that's praising without words. The bell holds the time.
Jaap Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise of the Timeless, in changing meters, said every Sikh morning after Japji.
Your line: the rhythm of praise. Today, when you hear a beat, in a song, in footsteps, in rain, let it remind you of Jaap's gallop, and give thanks for one thing. Day one hundred thirty.

131.title: Tav Prasad Savaiye
131.hook: ten verses saying that kings, armies and rituals are nothing without love
131.howItsDone: The ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, are recited every morning in Nitnem after Jaap Sahib, and are among the five banis of the Amrit ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaap Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh's galloping praise. Your line was the rhythm of praise. What beat reminded you of it? Today, the same Guru, in a very different mood. Day one hundred thirty-one.

Scroll any feed for five minutes and you'll see what the world calls impressive. The mansion. The supercar. The influencer at a holy site at sunrise, perfectly lit. Followers in the millions. Centuries ago a poet saw the equivalent of all that in his own day, the richest kings, the biggest armies, the most admired ascetics and pilgrims, and he wrote ten short poems that keep turning back to the same thought. All of it, he says, is worth nothing, without one thing.
screen: `THE MANSION, THE SUPERCAR.` → `THE PERFECT HOLY PHOTO.` → `ALL OF IT, WORTH NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The poems are the Tav Prasad Savaiye, the third bani of the Sikh morning. Tav prasad means by your grace. Savaiya is the name of the poetic form: a four-line verse with long, flowing lines, beautiful to recite. These ten come from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless, in the Dasam Granth. Each verse is a parade. In paraphrase: I have seen the pure ascetics, the yogis, the celibates, crowds of them. I have seen mighty kings riding elephants with golden trappings, great horses, armies without number, emperors who conquered the earth. I have seen pilgrims bathing at every holy river, people fasting, people performing every ritual. And then, as the verses close, the turn. Without the Lord, without love, none of it counts for anything. And the famous line, again in paraphrase: I tell the truth, listen, everyone: only those who loved found the Lord. Notice who is saying this. Guru Gobind Singh was himself a leader of armies, who knew horses and weapons and power from the inside. He's not sneering at kings from the outside. The savaiyas say, from someone who knew that world: it isn't the thing. Neither, they say, is outward religion done without love. The savaiyas are gentle with no one's pride, including the pride of the pious. What remains after the parade passes? Love. That's why these ten verses sit in the morning. Before the day starts measuring you by what you own or how you look, the savaiyas measure differently.
screen: `TAV PRASAD — BY YOUR GRACE.` · `A PARADE OF KINGS AND HOLY MEN.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND GOD.` · `A LEADER OF ARMIES SAYS IT.` · then, large: `WITHOUT LOVE, NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Listen to one savaiya. If you can, play a recording of Tav Prasad Savaiye and listen to just the first verse, about a minute. Notice the long, rolling lines. If you can't play one, try this instead: think of one thing you've been proud of lately, a promotion, a purchase, a good photo. Hold it for a moment. Then ask the savaiyas' question: was there love in it? No judgment. Just the question. The bell holds the time.
Savaiya. A four-line verse with long, flowing lines. Guru Gobind Singh's ten savaiyas keep returning to one thought: without love, nothing.
Your line: without love, nothing. Today, when something impressive crosses your screen, ask the savaiya's question: where's the love in it? Day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: Chaupai Sahib
132.hook: a prayer asking to be kept under the Guru's protecting hand
132.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib as part of the morning banis and within Rehras in the evening, and some say it at times of fear, before travel or at a hospital bedside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the savaiya, ten verses ending in love. Your line was without love, nothing. Did anything impressive cross your screen that the savaiyas would have weighed differently? Day one hundred thirty-two.

A child is crossing a busy road. Halfway across, without looking up, the small hand reaches out, and a bigger hand closes around it. Nobody has to say anything. Grown-ups have their own versions of that moment: a diagnosis, a turbulent flight, a phone call at two in the morning. Sikhs have a prayer that is built around that reach. Some say it every day, and some say it again when they're afraid. Today, Chaupai Sahib.
screen: `A SMALL HAND REACHES OUT.` → `TURBULENCE, A 2 A.M. CALL.` → `A PRAYER FOR THE REACH.`

segments.voice: Chaupai Sahib is by Guru Gobind Singh, and it comes from the Dasam Granth. Its full name is often given as Benti Chaupai: benti means a humble request, and chaupai is the verse form, short lines grouped in fours. It's recited in the morning by Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem, it's part of the evening Rehras, and it's one of the banis read at the Amrit ceremony. And the whole of it is one long request: keep me. The opening, in paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand; may the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Let my mind stay at your feet; cherish me as your own. Then the prayer widens. It asks to be kept from enemies, from harm, from those who would do wrong. It praises the One who creates and sustains everything, who knows each heart from inside. And it returns again and again to that picture of the hand. What's striking is that it's a request at all. Its author was the tenth Guru, and Sikh tradition remembers the hardships of his life: his father's execution, and later the deaths of his sons. Yet the prayer has no swagger in it. It speaks as someone asking to be carried. Some people, hearing a prayer for protection, expect it to promise nothing bad will happen. Chaupai doesn't promise that. The Guru's own life didn't look like that. What it asks for is to be held, to be counted as one of God's own, whatever comes. That's the reach the child makes on the road. Not a guarantee. A hand.
screen: `BENTI — A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `GIVE ME YOUR HAND.` · `A GURU WHO KNEW DANGER.` · `NOT A PROMISE: A HAND.` · then, large: `KEEP ME.`

segments.voice: If you can, find Chaupai Sahib, in a gutka, online, or as a recording, and read or hear its opening lines. Let them be slow. If you can't, simply sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up. Think of one thing you're carrying right now that feels too heavy. If you pray, you can hold it up in the words of Chaupai's opening request: protect me, giving me your hand. If you don't, just let your open hands hold it for a while. The bell holds the time.
Chaupai Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh's prayer in four-line verses, asking to be kept under God's protecting hand.
Your line: keep me. Today, in one anxious moment, open your hand at your side, just slightly, and remember the reach. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: Anand Sahib
133.hook: Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, part of the morning or evening prayers
133.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite all forty pauris of Anand Sahib in the morning; its short form of six pauris is sung near the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, before Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaupai Sahib, the prayer for a hand. Your line was keep me. This week: your simran, Nitnem, Japji at dawn, Jaap's gallop, the savaiyas, Chaupai. Today the morning set is complete. Day one hundred thirty-three.
screen: `YOUR SIMRAN · NITNEM · JAPJI · JAAP · SAVAIYAS · CHAUPAI.`

segments.voice: A wedding. A child's naming. A memorial. An ordinary Sunday service. Four very different mornings in a gurdwara, and near the end of each one, the same short song. The Sikh code of conduct asks for it at the close of services, so it's sung over happy occasions and sad ones alike, and then everyone stands for the prayer called Ardas. It's the song of bliss, written by the third Guru. Today, Anand Sahib.
screen: `A WEDDING, A NAMING, A MEMORIAL.` → `THE SAME SONG NEAR THE END.` → `THE SONG OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: Anand means bliss, deep joy. Anand Sahib is by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and it's in the Guru Granth Sahib in Raag Ramkali: forty pauris. Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite all forty in the morning, after Chaupai. A shorter form, the first five pauris and the last, is sung at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, and part of it is said in the evening Rehras too. The first line is where the whole song lives. In paraphrase: joy has come, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. Notice who the line is spoken to. Not a crowd. O my mother. It sounds like someone bursting through the kitchen door with news. And notice the tense. Joy has come. It isn't a wish. It's something that happened. The line goes on to say the Guru was found with sahaj, with ease, naturally, and that the heart is filled with music. Then the pauris turn the joy over, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. What is real joy? Everyone talks about bliss, the song says, but bliss is known through the Guru. True anand comes from the Name and the Guru's word, and the song asks the listener to sing that word. So this bliss isn't the same as having no troubles. That's how it can be sung at funerals as well as weddings: the joy it names sits underneath, a sense of having been found. Guru Amar Das found his Guru late: tradition says he was already in his sixties. Joy, found, even then.
screen: `ANAND — BLISS, DEEP JOY.` · `JOY HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.` · `FOUND WITH EASE, SAHAJ.` · `AT WEDDINGS AND AT FUNERALS.` · then, large: `JOY, FOUND.`

segments.voice: Listen to Anand Sahib's first pauri. If you can, play a recording now, about a minute of it. Let the opening line land: joy has come, O my mother. If you can't play it, try this: remember a moment when you ran to tell someone good news. Who did you tell? What did it feel like to say it out loud? Sit inside that moment, and then let it settle into something quieter. The bell holds the time.
Anand Sahib. Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, forty pauris, whose short form closes Sikh services and ceremonies.
Your line: joy, found. Today, tell one person about one good thing, the way you'd burst through the door to tell your mother. Day one hundred thirty-three.
